system_prompt:
You are distilling one chapter of a guitar method book into a short summary.

The user will give you a chapter file with topic-organized verbatim quotes
plus the human-rationale notes for each. Write a one-paragraph summary (4-7
sentences) that captures:

  - what this chapter teaches (the techniques, concepts, rules, examples)
  - the master's characteristic moves visible in this chapter (if any)
  - the load-bearing terminology this chapter introduces

Reference the topic labels from the chapter file when useful. Do not invent
information not present in the chapter. If the chapter is biographical or
introductory rather than instructional, say so explicitly.

Output just the paragraph — no preamble, no JSON, no markdown formatting.

<<<CHAPTER FILE
# Chapter 3 — WELCOME TO VOLUME II

_Pages 7-8._

> **Verbatim-quote constraint.** The quotes below are exact substrings of the raw transcript produced by `pdftotext`. The transcript may contain extraction artifacts where the book's typeface confuses the tool — e.g. `7irst` or `<irst` for `first`, `speci7ic` for `specific`. **Do NOT manually fix these in this file**: the quote-fidelity validator compares against the raw transcript, so a 'fixed' quote will fail verification and break Stage 2 idempotency. If a future pipeline iteration adds artifact-normalization, it must normalize the transcript and these files together.

## Volume II chord naming rationale

> the reason that all the chords in Volume II are left nameless is that the names one
> might use get complicated. [Cmaj9th(noSth), for example.] Also, these names could easily tend
> to limit how the chords could be used.

**Significance (p. 7).** Explains the deliberate methodological choice to omit chord names in Volume II.

## 4ths and 2nds chord ambiguity

> Since the chords in Volume II revolve around structures of
> 4th intervals and 2nd intervals, they are more ambiguous sounding than the structures in Vol-
> ume I. Also, in many cases they are more flexible in terms of multiple functions.

**Significance (p. 7).** Defines the sonic and functional character of Volume II's harmonic vocabulary.

## Volume II retroactive application

> it would be good to keep in mind that many of the ideas in this text for
> Volume II are retroactive. That is to say that they apply to both books.

**Significance (p. 8).** Critical usage rule telling the reader to apply Volume II concepts retrospectively to Volume I.

## Volume II content overview

> Volume II contains 3-part 4ths, 4-part 4ths and spread clusters voice-led through all 6
> cycles in C Major, C Melodic Minor and C Harmonic Minor.

**Significance (p. 8).** Enumerates the structural content and three scale systems organizing the book.

## Volume I triad-based architecture

> If you look at all of the material in Volume I, you would see that
> it’s all triad-based. The triads are triads. The 7th chords are a triad plus another note. TBN Lis a
> triad plus another note. And TBN II is also a triad plus another note.

**Significance (p. 8).** Provides the unifying structural definition of Volume I's chord vocabulary.

## Five families of 4-part chords

> you've got the complete set of 5 families of 4-part chords: 7th, TBN I, TBN IL, 4
> part 4th, Spread Cluster.

**Significance (p. 8).** Names the exhaustive taxonomy of 4-part chord families used in the method.

## Completeness claim for diatonic scales

> THERE ARE NO OTHER TYPES OF 4-PART* CHORD FAMILIES WITHIN THE 3
> DIATONIC 7-NOTE SCALES WE ARE WORKING WITH!!! (MAJOR, MELODIC MINOR,
> HARMONIC MINOR) {*4-part being defined as “containing 4 different notes”}

**Significance (p. 8).** Explicit theoretical completeness claim that justifies the method's scope.

CHAPTER FILE>>>
